body:
What happens: `assets/posts/tormach-lathe.cps` (`g76Grid`) takes J (first depth) to the grid with `floor` and K from the rounded peak and outward-rounded root, each on its own. LinuxCNC's `R1` (constant depth) ladder cuts J, 2J, ... clamped at K, so it cuts ceil(K/J) passes. The inch golden `crates/app/tests/golden/nc/tormach-lathe/thread_g76_inch.nc` posts `G76 P0.07874 Z0.315 I-0.004 J0.0314 K0.0944 R1 Q0 H0`: 0.0944 / 0.0314 = 3.006, so the control cuts 0.0314, 0.0628, 0.0942 and a 0.0944 pass (0.0002 in on diameter), 4 passes where the record laid and the verdict judged 3 (0.4 / 0.8 / 1.2 mm radius). The mm golden (`J0.8 K2.4`) is exact.

Not a gouge: the extra pass is shallower than the root and the root is rounded outward. But the posted words state a pass schedule that was not verified, the same class of mismatch #417 removes on the Fanuc lathe (PR #517 review, where the Fanuc inch R was fixed by deriving it from the rounded words' own ladder).

Expected: the grid words' own ladder cuts exactly the record's pass count: e.g. choose J (and K within the outward-root rule) so ceil(K/J) equals the record's rung count, or refuse by name when the grid cannot state it. Semantics from the LinuxCNC G76 documentation (R1 = constant depth, K = full depth).

Note: the inch golden was run on the PathPilot Hub 8L sim to M30 with no alarm (PR #517 comments); that run does not check the pass count. A fix changes that golden and needs a new Hub run.

Found while fixing the M3 review of PR #517 (#417); left out of that PR because its Tormach goldens must stay byte-identical to main.

Done means: the Tormach inch G76 words make LinuxCNC's ladder cut exactly the record's passes (a test parses the posted J/K and counts ceil(K/J) against the record), or the record is refused by name; mm output unchanged.

body:
What happens: a STEP solid whose faces are all wound inward (consistently, so no face disagrees with a neighbour) imports with a negative signed volume. Nothing flips it and nothing says so. Seen with the local older test part `step-block-371.step` (20 facets, V = -102000 mm^3) on upstream main and on the #1576 branch alike, found in the review of PR #1576 (issue #1573). A synthetic stand-in reproduces it: `testdata/models/box.step` with every `same_sense` (FACE_SURFACE and FACE_BOUND) inverted imports with V = -1, `notes = []`.

Why #1576 leaves it: its rule flips faces only where neighbours disagree, so a consistently inverted shell is untouched. Deciding "outward" when nothing flipped is wrong for an open or lone-face shell (a curved open face's centroid volume has no meaning), so it needs a guard: closed, gap-free (the seams judge already knows) and every shared edge opposite.

What a wrong winding can do, as far as traced:
- `crates/app/src/pick/winding.rs` already refuses face picks on a wound-inward body by name, so alignment to it is refused, not wrong.
- The solid law (`crates/sim/src/verify/solid.rs`) reads the mesh by ray parity, which does not depend on winding, so the gouge check is not fooled on this evidence.
- NOT traced: generators or checks that read facet normals directly (3D finishing, pocket3d offsets, tool-side). Whoever works this should grep them and test one op on an inverted box; if any gouges or cuts the wrong side, raise to P1.

Rating: P3 (wrong behaviour a user hits, with a workaround: re-export or import an STL; the picks refuse). By the AGENTS.md safety floor the fix touches geometry, so effort:high.

Done means: a closed, gap-free STEP shell with every shared edge opposite and a negative signed volume is flipped outward at import and says so in the import notes (the `Graded`/MCP `notes` and status line); an open or lone-face shell is left alone; pinning tests for the inverted box and for the lone-curved-face case; the unchecked normal-reading ops listed above are checked against an inverted box and the result is commented here.

Part of / refs: #1573 (closed-shell watertight), found in the review of PR #1576.

title: Mill posts: the first traverse after a tool change does not state its clearance Z (grblhal, carvera; fanuc-family combined first rapid)

labels.name: P1

labels.name: area:post

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
Found while fixing #1614, the same hazard in the other mill posts.

**The hazard (#1614, from a PathPilot Hub run).** After a tool change the spindle stands at the top of Z travel. With a long tool on a high work offset, the tip can stand below the part top there. A first X/Y move that does not first state a clearance height then crosses the part. `tormach.cps` now writes `G0 Z<ClearancePlane>` (else the `RetractPlane`) before the first X/Y traverse. A setup that cannot clear is then stopped by the control's Z limit, not rapided through the part. A stream that states neither plane is refused by name.

**Same pattern elsewhere** (from the synth goldens, `crates/app/tests/golden/nc/synth_*.nc`):
- `grblhal.cps`, `carvera.cps`: `T2 M6` ... `G0 X20 Y10` is a bare X/Y traverse at whatever height the tool change left, then `G0 X20 Y10 Z-3`. This is exactly the #1614 shape.
- `fanuc.cps`, `haas.cps`, `mazak.cps`, `doosan-dnm.cps`, `sinumerik.cps`, `heidenhain.cps`: after `G43 H..`, the first block is the stream's first rapid as one combined move, `G00 X20 Y10 Z-3`. It goes in a straight line from the tool-change height. It is safe only while that start height is above the part. With a tool too long for the work offset, the line starts below the part top.
- `tinyg.cps`: check it too (it lifts with `G53 G0 Z0` after `M0`, then traverses).

**Done means:** each spindle mill post states the section's clearance Z (a Z-only rapid to `ClearancePlane`, else `RetractPlane`) before its first X/Y motion after a tool change and at the program start. A stream stating neither is refused by name. There is a pinning test per post. Moved goldens are regenerated and listed in the PR (expect one added `G0 Z` line per program, as #1614 saw across 32 Tormach goldens).

Part of the #1614 follow-up.

title: Tormach post: the first XY traverse after a tool change rides at the top of Z even when that is below the part's clearance (Hub: down, over, up)

labels.name: P1
labels.description: Unsafe or wrong output: gouge, collision, wrong G-code, crash, data loss; blocks a cut

labels.name: area:post
labels.description: Post processors and G-code

labels.name: in-review
labels.description: Fix pushed on a branch with an open PR; merges at the next cut

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
**Found in a PathPilot Hub run (770MX sim, v2.14.4, 2026-11-13)** of the merged #1357 golden `crates/app/tests/golden/nc/tormach/drill_peck.nc`, posted inch for the 770MX.

**What happened.** In Hub's tool table T4 is 5.0000" long. With the session's G54 Z zero, the top of Z travel was only about 4.3" above work Z0. The program runs:

```
G53 G0 Z0        (top of travel)
G30
T4 M6
G43 H4           (5" tool: the tip is now about 0.68" BELOW work Z0, though nothing moved)
S1500 M3
M8
G0 X0.7874 Y0.3937       <- the XY traverse at that height: below the part top
G0 X0.7874 Y0.3937 Z0    <- then UP to Z0
```

The user saw the tool go down, then over, then up. "Down" is the 5" length offset taking effect. "Over" is the XY rapid with the tip about 0.68" below the stock surface. "Up" is the rapid to Z0. On a real machine that traverse would drive the tool through the part or the vise. At load time PathPilot warned "Program exceeds machine maximum on Z axis by 0.5107 in (line 0)", but the post still writes a traverse that cannot clear.

**Cause.** `tormach.cps` (`xyFirst` / `startXY`) makes the first XY move after a tool change "at the current - safe, Z-up - height". It assumes the top of travel is above the part. It never states the section's clearance Z before the traverse. When the tool is too long for the work offset, the top of travel is below that clearance.

**Proposed fix.** After `G43 H..`, and before the first XY traverse, write `G0 Z<clearance>` from the section's `ClearancePlane` (or its first rapid's Z). On a setup that can clear, this is an ordinary move down to clearance. On a setup that cannot, the control refuses the block as beyond its Z limit and stops. That is a visible refusal, not a rapid through the part. Pin it with a test: a stream whose first XY rapid follows a tool change shows `G0 Z<clearance>` before it. Regenerate the Tormach goldens this moves (listed in the PR). Check whether the other mill posts share the assumption, and file each one that does.

**Done means:** no Tormach program makes its first XY traverse after a tool change without first stating the clearance Z. That is pinned by a test, and the moved goldens are listed in the PR.

Related: #1357 (merged), the Hub session screenshots of 2026-11-13 17:55.

title: post-merge.yml: the report job is skipped when the gate fails, so a red main opens no issue

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: area:build
labels.description: Build, CI, release, tests

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:low
labels.description: Mechanical, one file, no new logic (issue-worker-low)

labels.name: P5
labels.description: Agent surface and tooling keep up with what shipped

body:
What happens: post-merge run 43535610115 (push to main at 745edc36a) ended with job `gate` = failure and job `report` = skipped. The rolling issue `main is red (post-merge gate)` was not opened or commented on.

Expected: AGENTS.md "Fixes are tested in the background": a red post-merge gate opens or comments on the rolling issue; the next green run closes it.

Cause (read from `.github/workflows/post-merge.yml` on main): the `report` job has `needs: gate` and an `if:` with no status-check function:

```
if: ${{ (needs.gate.result == 'success' || needs.gate.result == 'failure') && needs.gate.outputs.skipped != 'true' && (...) }}
```

GitHub Actions adds an implicit `success()` to a job's `if` unless it contains `always()`, `failure()`, `cancelled()` or `!cancelled()`. With a failed `needs` job the implicit `success()` is false, so the job is skipped before the expression is read. The job therefore only ever runs on green.

Suggested fix: start the condition with `always() &&` (the rest already excludes cancelled and skipped runs). One line.

Note on this particular run: its only red test was `a_lowered_cap_refuses_the_same_face_at_once` (`crates/app/tests/import_step_guard.rs`, "not within 30s"), the wall-clock flake of issue 1605, so main was not truly red here. The reporting gap is real for any failure.

A `.github/` change: the PR is read, not built, and waits for the maintainer (`needs-maintainer`). `Process change: yes` does not apply (`.github/` is not a process file).

Found by the maintenance session while watching runs.

Done means: a post-merge run whose gate fails runs `report` and opens or comments on the rolling issue; a green run after it closes that issue; a cancelled or cut-skipped run still reports nothing.

When the stock holds a part and the cut reaches into it, the operation has 0 findings. Found while working #1595 / #1603 (branch `issue/1595-engrave-law`, upstream main 745edc36 plus that branch).

**Probe:** the #1585 fixture (40 x 40 x 8 block, R15 pocket to Z4, EM-0600-4FL) in a 40 x 40 x 8 box stock centred over it. Engrave / Trace, source `Stock`, Top Z8, Bottom Z1 (the stock's outline is the part's outline, so the line runs down the part's outside wall):

|---|---|---|---|
| Engrave | 0 | blocked by the program sim ("worst 7.00 mm") | **posts** |
| Trace | 0 | blocked by the program sim ("worst 7.00 mm") | **posts** |

body:
What happens: `a_finer_pass_that_runs_out_on_a_face_that_may_jump_is_refused` in `crates/app/tests/import_step_guard.rs:36` failed in pr-test run 43533416032 (PR 1598) with "import did not finish within 30s - the hang is back". PR 1598 touches no import or STEP code; the self-hosted runner was running another gate and a post-merge run at the same time. Motion and ui suites passed.

Why it matters: the test pins the hang guard for untrusted STEP files with a wall-clock limit, so a busy runner turns an unrelated PR's quick gate red and the review cannot be proven by a build.

Not proven: that load is the cause. No completed post-merge run on main shows the test green or red at that moment.

**What happens:** whole-model 2D Pocket and 2D Adaptive (and the stock-source Adaptive of #1554) can cut into the part with **no finding on the op**. On a **turned (rotated) stock** the post goes out, because the program sim refuses to judge a turned stock and nothing else catches it. Found by M5's review of PR #1597 (pullrequestreview-5899991928), on upstream main be27a4c7 plus #1597.

| Case | Depth into the part | Op findings | Aligned stock | Turned stock |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pocket / Adaptive2D, whole-model source, Area offset +3 | 4.0-4.25 mm | 0 | blocked by the program sim | **posts** |
| Pocket / Adaptive2D, whole-model source, extension +5 | 5 mm | 0 | blocked by the program sim | **posts** |
| #1554: stock-source Adaptive2D / Pocket | 7 mm | 0 | blocked by the program sim | **posts** |

Same root as #1595 (Engrave/Trace) and the TrochoidalSlot gap fixed by #1597. This is a gouge that passes on a turned stock: P1.

Legal whole-model pockets with default controls must still post. That is why #1597 did not simply make `uncovered()` refuse every None-law op.

**Done means:** the three rows above are refused (on the op, and the post is blocked) with the stock aligned and turned; legal whole-model pockets and adaptives with default controls still post on both. Pinned through `operation::generate` and the post, mutation-checked.

body:
Found while working #1509.

What happens: the stand-alone Trochoidal slot bores its entry helix on a circle of the loop band's half-width `b = (W - D) / 2 - leave` about the centre line's start (`crates/motion/src/machining2d/trochoid_bore.rs`, the plain bore; before #1509's PR the same code in `trochoid_slot.rs`, `emit_level`). A helix of radius `b` clears the ring `b +- r`. With `b > r` (a slot wider than twice the tool: W > 2 D) a post of radius `b - r` is left standing at the bore's centre, full depth. No front arc reaches it (the loops only advance away from the bore), the operation reports OK, and the verifier has nothing to say (uncut material is not a gouge).

Evidence: on a band of half-width 4.9 mm with a 6 mm tool (post radius 1.9 mm), the plain bore leaves more than 4 mm2 standing inside a 1.4 mm disc about the start, read on the dexel stock (`quality::rest_area`); the test `the_opened_bore_leaves_no_post_at_the_lane_start` in `crates/motion/src/machining2d/adaptive_troch_tests.rs` asserts it for the plain bore and its absence for the opened one. The maintainer's #1503 screenshot (W 16, D 6: b = 5, r = 3) has a 2 mm radius post at A.

Expected: no post. The 2D Adaptive trochoidal method already opens its bore (`trochoid_bore::bore` with `open: true`: helix at half the tool radius, then a two-centre semicircle spiral out to the band, read by the same engagement measurement). The stand-alone slot can take the same bore; that moves its output for W > 2 D (its golden `trochoid_slot_small.cl` has b < r and does not move).

Follow-up to #1315 (PR #1485), tested on macOS 27 (Apple silicon) with `/bin/bash` 3.2 and BSD sed at `0b4052bb`.

**What happens:** after #1485, the script gets through the sysroot download, the `shasum` check and the `sed` patching on macOS. The link of `camcraft-cli` then fails with `rust-lld: error: … undefined symbol: ecs_has_id` (and `ecs_modified_id`, `ecs_cpp_set`, …). **Suggested change:** on macOS, when `AR_wasm32_unknown_unknown` isn't set, the script finds `llvm-ar` (on PATH, Homebrew's `$(brew --prefix llvm)/bin`, or rustup's `llvm-tools`) and exports it. With none found, it stops with a message naming what to install (`brew install llvm` or `rustup component add llvm-tools`) instead of failing at the link. "Needs:" in the header gains `llvm-ar` on macOS.

**Done means:** #1315's own definition of done. `web/build-app-wasm.sh` and `web/check-app-page.sh` run unmodified on macOS with `/bin/bash` and BSD sed.

title: Circular writes each ring as 512 chords with no arcs: one 6 mm hole is 74,131 moves

body:
Found while programming a simple 2.5D end-cap plate (user's project) with the CamCraft **v0.19.0** release CLI (macOS arm64), driven headlessly over MCP. Re-checked on upstream main **d00243a5**: **still reproduces, identical move counts**.

## What happens

One Ø6 mm through hole (10 mm deep plate, 11 mm cut) with a Circular op and a 4 mm end mill came out as **74,131 moves** (53 rapids, 74,078 feeds, median feed length **0.0061 mm**, no arcs). Posted, that is about 74,000 G1 blocks for one small hole: a huge file, and at 500 mm/min each block lasts under 1 ms, far past what most controls can process, so the machine starves and stutters. The user dropped Circular and used the Bore op (arcs) instead.

Every parameter set tried is in the tens of thousands:

| Circular params (others as below) | moves | median segment |
|---|---|---|
| as below (helix entry R1, stepover 0.5) | 74,131 | 0.0061 mm |
| `entry: plunge` | 13,416 | 0.0123 mm |
| `helix_radius: 0.5` | 13,446 | 0.0123 mm (+ warnings `feed moves 2 and 6737 cross in XY at shared depth`) |
| `stepover: 1.0` or `2.0` | 26,937 | 0.0123 mm |
| `radius: 4.0` | 26,858 | 0.0184 mm |
| `radius: 6.0` | 53,690 | 0.0307 mm |
| `stepdown: 2.0` | 67,989 | 0.0061 mm |

**Cause (read, not fixed).** `ring_loop` in `crates/motion/src/machining2d/circular.rs` writes every ring as a closed polygon of **512 chords** whatever its radius, and the op emits no arcs. A ring at R1 (6 mm hole, 4 mm tool) is 512 chords of 0.012 mm each, at every level. The helix entry ("stands down to a ramp along the first cut") then ramps along that polygon, splitting it further, which is where the 74k comes from. The Bore op on the same hole emits three arcs per ring.

## Minimal repro (MCP)

```
import_model   {"path": "End Caps-End capSupport Plate.step", "name": "part"}
move_model     {"name": "part", "position": [0, 37.9, 4.826]}
add_setup      {"name": "Setup 1"}
set_stock      {"box": {"dx": 110, "dy": 185, "dz": 15.33}}
set_wcs        {"stock_point": {"x": "center", "y": "center", "z": "max"}}
add_tool       {"catalog": "EM-0400-2FL", "name": "EM4"}
add_operation  {"kind": "Circular", "tool": "EM4", "name": "c", "source": "part",
                "params": {"center": [-35.0, 2.9], "radius": 3.0, "stepover": 0.5,
                           "top_z": {"reference": "top_of_stock", "offset": -0.508},
                           "bottom_z": {"reference": "top_of_stock", "offset": -11.524},
                           "stepdown": 1.0, "feed": 500, "plunge_feed": 250, "climb": true,
                           "entry": "helix", "helix_radius": 1.0}}
generate {}   -> 74,131 moves
```

(The project used inch units; these are the same values in mm. Any model and any small circle show it; the hole position is one of the plate's Ø6 holes.)

## Expected

A Circular ring posts as true arcs (G2/G3, a few per ring, as Bore does), and the helix or ramp entry as a helical arc or a few segments; a hole like this is a few hundred blocks at most. Where chords are needed, their count comes from a chord tolerance, not a fixed 512.

## Done means

- The repro above generates under ~500 moves with the rings as arcs; the move count is pinned by a test (with a ceiling per ring and level).
- Path and verify results otherwise unchanged (same radii, depths and direction); CL/NC goldens for Circular regenerated in one commit.

| 2D Contour, inside (bore) | CW | **no** (conventional) |
| 2D Pocket, bore wall pass | CW | **no** (conventional) |
| 2D Adaptive, in the bore | CCW (G3) | yes |
| Bore | CCW (G3) | yes |
| Circular | CCW | yes |

Posted output (main, outside contour, `climb: true`; the part spans X ±50, Y ±30):

```
S9500 M3
...
G01 X50.346 Y-32.98 Z-2 F1200
G03 X53 Y-30 Z-2 I-0.346 J2.98 F1200
G01 X53 Y30 Z-2 F1200
G03 X50 Y33 Z-2 I-3 J0 F1200
G01 X-50 Y33 Z-2 F1200
```

That is the tool going up the +X side and across the top to -X: CCW around the part.

**The convention.** With M3 (clockwise spindle seen from above), climb milling keeps the material on the **right** of the tool's travel (the G41 side): an outside profile runs **clockwise** around the part, an inside profile (a hole or pocket wall) runs **counter-clockwise**. Conventional is the reverse. With M4 both reverse.

**Cause (read, not fixed).** `crates/motion/src/machining2d/contour.rs` (around line 207) says "Canonical orientation is material-on-the-left travel; conventional climbing reverses it", and keeps that order when `p.climb != inside`. Material on the left of the travel with M3 is conventional, so the rule is inverted. The unit test `contour_inside_shrinks_and_flips_travel` in `machining2d/tests.rs` pins the same reading ("climb under Inside travels the loop reversed, so material stays on the left"). The GUI label maps 1:1 to the parameter, so the parameter, not the label, is what is wrong. The pocket's wall pass needs the same check (`pocket.rs` / `pocket_hsm.rs` `plan_passes`); also worth checking 2D Chamfer, Slot, Trace and the contour lead/arc side (`arc_leads.rs` `air_side`), which follow the same flag.

## Minimal repro (MCP)

`plate_bore.stl`: a 100 x 60 x 10 mm plate, centred in XY, z 0..10, with a centred Ø40 through bore.

```
import_model   {"path": "plate_bore.stl", "name": "plate"}
add_setup      {"name": "Setup 1"}
set_stock      {"box": {"dx": 120, "dy": 80, "dz": 12}}
set_wcs        {"stock_point": {"x": "center", "y": "center", "z": "max"}}
add_tool       {"catalog": "EM-0600-4FL", "name": "EM6"}
add_operation  {"kind": "2D Contour", "tool": "EM6", "name": "outside", "source": "plate",
                "params": {"top_z": {"reference": "top_of_stock", "offset": -2},
                           "bottom_z": {"reference": "top_of_stock", "offset": -11},
                           "stepdown": 20, "climb": true, "entry": "plunge"}}
set_operation_geometry {"operation": "outside", "picks": [the 4 top outer edges' chains]}
edit_operation {"name": "outside", "params": {"side": "outside"}}
(same again, "inside", picking the bore's top chain, side "inside")
generate {} ; post {"output": "out.nc"}
```

Result: outside CCW, inside CW (signed area of the floor-level feed moves +7276 / -915 mm²). With `climb: false`: outside CW, inside CCW.

## Expected

`climb: true` with M3: outside profiles CW, inside profiles CCW, on every 2D op that takes the flag (and both reversed under M4), matching Adaptive, Bore and Circular today.

## Done means

- 2D Contour (outside, inside, open chains) and the 2D Pocket wall pass run climb as defined above when `climb: true`, conventional when false; pinned by a direction test per op that checks the signed travel at a level against the spindle direction.
- Every other op with a `climb` flag (Chamfer, Slot, Trace, Face rows, leads) checked against the same rule and pinned.
- The test that pins "material on the left" is corrected, not deleted; affected CL/NC goldens are regenerated in one commit.
- The release notes say that contour and pocket direction changed: a project that set `climb: false` as a workaround will now post conventional.

## What happens

A 2D Adaptive with `source: "stock"` and no geometry picks clears the **whole stock footprint**, the part included, to full depth. `generate` reports the op `ok` with no warning and no note. Only `verify` catches it, and blocks the post:

- the user's plate: `gouge: program cuts below the model in 85918 cell(s), worst 11.02 mm`. Same with an exclude boundary on the bore, and with the part unrotated.
- the minimal repro below (a plain 100 x 60 x 10 box, no bore at all): `gouge: program cuts below the model in 42560 cell(s), worst 9.00 mm at (-49.69, -29.69, z 1.00)`. With a centred Ø40 bore in it: 33634 cells, worst 9.00 mm. 1066 of the 1740 feed points sit inside the part outline below its top.

Nothing unsafe is posted (verify holds the post). But generate hands back a path that cuts through the part and calls it `ok`.

**Second finding, same goal (rough a plate's outside in a slightly larger stock).** With `source: "plate"` (the model) the adaptive does protect the part. But when the stock margin is narrower than the tool (3.175 mm per side with a 6 mm tool, the user's 0.125 in), the outside band is **dropped silently**: the op comes back `ok` with no note and no warnings, and every one of its 51,188 feed points is inside the bore; the outside is not cut at all. The user's attempt to limit the adaptive to that band with picks was refused instead: `pocket is narrower than the tool`. An outside band is open to air on its outer side, so a tool wider than the band can still cut it (one pass along the part, hanging over the stock edge).

## Minimal repro (MCP)

`plate.stl`: a closed 100 x 60 x 10 mm box, centred in XY, z 0..10 (12 facets).

```

add_setup      {"name": "Setup 1"}
set_stock      {"box": {"dx": 120, "dy": 80, "dz": 12}}
set_wcs        {"stock_point": {"x": "center", "y": "center", "z": "max"}}
add_tool       {"catalog": "EM-0600-4FL", "name": "EM6"}
add_operation  {"kind": "2D Adaptive", "tool": "EM6", "name": "outside rough", "source": "stock",
                "params": {"top_z": {"reference": "top_of_stock", "offset": 0},
                           "bottom_z": {"reference": "top_of_stock", "offset": -11}, "stepdown": 4}}
generate {}   -> status "ok", 882 moves, 0 warnings
verify {}     -> ok: false, "gouge: program cuts below the model in 42560 cell(s), worst 9.00 mm ..."
```

Same calls with `"source": "plate"`: 318 moves, all outside the part, verify clean (the expected behaviour). With `"source": "plate"`, a Ø40 bore in the plate and the stock at 106.35 x 66.35 (3.175 mm margin): `ok`, no note, the outside not cut.

## Expected

- A stock-sourced 2D Adaptive in a setup that holds a part never machines the part's own section: it roughs the stock minus the part (the outside band, and nothing inside the part outline unless picked), or it refuses at generate by name ("the stock source covers the part - pick the area or use the model as the source"). Compare #12 (the same law for a whole-model Pocket source) and #3.
- An outside band narrower than the tool is still roughed (the tool may hang over the open stock edge), or the op says plainly that the band was skipped and why. Never a silent `ok` that left the outside uncut.

## Done means

- The minimal repro above (stock source, plain box) generates a path with no cut inside the part outline below its top, or is refused at generate with a message naming the cause; pinned by a test.

title: Second setups: fixtures in a flipped (aligned) setup are judged by bounding box

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: P2

body:
Found while programming a small two-sided part with HAT-style stock and soft jaws (user's project), with the CamCraft **v0.19.0** release CLI (macOS arm64), driven headlessly over MCP.

## What happens

In a second setup that takes "what Setup 1 leaves behind" as its stock (part flipped, part alignment), the carried-workholding gate judges each fixture by its **world bounding box**, not its shape. Any fixture whose box encloses the carried part is refused, even when the steel only touches the part's sides.

Cause (v0.19.0): `crates/app/src/fixture_carried.rs::carried_fixture_problems` reads `model::entity_world_aabb(world, &fe)` and passes that box to `penetration()`. Every carried column whose centre lies inside the box's XY footprint and whose material overlaps its Z span counts as a hit.

Refusals seen:

1. **The built-in vise** (`add_builtin_vise`, 5 in, jaws closed on a 50 mm part): its box spans the opening between the jaws, so the part it clamps "stands inside" it.
   `setup 'Setup 2': fixture 'Vise 5 in (2)' stands inside the stock carried from setup 'Setup 1' (4.48 mm deep) - the part that setup leaves cannot be held as modelled; move the fixture or re-check the hold`
2. **A pair of 5.2 x 2 x 1 in aluminum soft jaws with a nest pocket**, imported as one STEP fixture, with the part seated in the nest:
   `fixture 'Soft jaws (nest)' stands inside the stock carried from setup 'Setup 1' (11.43 mm deep) - the part that setup leaves cannot be held as modelled`
   The nest is inside the jaws' box, so the part is "inside the fixture" by definition.
3. The same jaws modelled as 9 plain blocks cut around the nest: the jaw "island" blocks are still refused at **9.93 and 11.28 mm** deep. Those island blocks lie inside the nest's L-shaped notch, below the part's notch floor (3.57 mm clearance as designed). Part of this may be that the Setup 1 3D ops were held, so the carried body there is not fully cut. The box-based judging is the same either way.

The workaround in the user's h5 project: model the vise jaws as two separate blocks instead of the built-in vise.

## Reproduction (headless, `camcraft-cli mcp`)

- The h5 plate: a 50 x 50 x 6 mm plate with 5 mm grooves.
- Setup 1 (top side) machines it from 55 x 55 x 11.3 mm stock in a vise.
- Setup 2 flips it about X (part alignment), uses "what Setup 1 leaves behind", and holds it in two block jaws plus parallels. That verifies and posts clean.
- Then, in Setup 2, place the built-in vise where the block jaws are:

```
open_project {path: h5.camproj}
add_builtin_vise {size: "5 in", setup: "Setup 2", position: [0, 25, -28.798], opening: 50}
verify
post {output: o.nc}
```

-> `verify.gate.problems` and the post refusal: `setup 'Setup 2': fixture 'Vise 5 in (2)' stands inside the stock carried from setup 'Setup 1' (4.48 mm deep) ...`

The vise's jaw faces are at Y +/-25, exactly the part's 50 mm sides. The steel only touches the part; the box reaches across it.

## Expected

The carried-stock fixture check judges the fixture's **real solid**: its mesh, or each body of a multi-body fixture, such as each jaw of a vise or each jaw of a soft-jaw pair. A part seated in a nest pocket, or clamped between jaws, passes. Steel truly inside the carried material is still refused by name.

**Done means:** a built-in vise clamping a carried part on its sides, and an imported soft-jaw fixture with a nest the carried part sits in, both pass the carried-workholding gate. A fixture that really overlaps the carried material (a jaw block moved into the part) is still refused with its depth. Pinning tests cover all three.

Not checked here: whether the in-setup fixture collision check (toolpath vs fixture) has the same box-only limit. It passed for the nest program in a single setup.

Related: #321 (the carried-workholding clause), #637 (carried stock on the field engine), #1511 (soft-jaw presets with a nest).

title: Work offsets: core uses an index, the post supplies the word and display name

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: area:post
labels.description: Post processors and G-code

labels.name: area:ui
labels.description: User interface and picking

labels.name: area:mcp
labels.description: MCP server and agent tooling (crates/app/src/mcp, camcraft-mcp skill)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

labels.name: P5
labels.description: Agent surface and tooling keep up with what shipped

body:
## Problem

A setup stores its work offset as an index (`SetupDef::work_offset`), but core
turns that index into a Fanuc-style word before any post is involved:

- The table `WCS_SLOTS = ["G54".."G59"]` lives in `camcraft-app`
  (`operation/types/sel.rs`) and is read directly by the Setups page combo,
  `setup::wcs_label`, the setup sheet, the MCP `set_work_offset` tool and the
  refusal messages.
- `posting::wcs_context` writes the word, not the index, into the stream as
  `PARAM WorkOffset`. Posts then parse it back: Fanuc and Mazak use
  `slotOf("G55") -> 1`, Heidenhain regex-matches `^G5([4-9])$` to pick a preset
  row.
- An index of 6 or more is refused in core, so extended offsets
  (`G54.1 P..`, Sinumerik `G505+`, further Heidenhain preset rows) cannot be
  expressed.

A setup with no machine and no post still shows `G54`: the word comes from
neither. Every other ask in the stream is already dialect-neutral (coolant,
after-operation); the work offset is the exception.

## Proposal

1. **Stream carries the index.** `PARAM WorkOffset` becomes a 1-based number.
   A manifest flag (`workOffsetIndex = true`) opts a script in, following the
   `coolantModes` / `afterModes` pattern. A script without the flag keeps
   receiving the word for offsets 1-6, so user-loaded posts keep working, and
   is refused by setup name for any offset above 6.
2. **Each post maps the index to its own word** and refuses, by setup name,
   an index it cannot express. The limit becomes the post's, not core's.
3. **The post supplies the display name.** A script may define a function
   (for example `workOffsetName(n)`) returning what the control calls offset
   `n` ("G55", "G54.1 P3", "preset 2"). The UI, setup sheet, MCP tool and
   refusal messages show "WCS n (name)" for the setup's resolved post.
4. **Fallback.** A script that defines no name function shows plain "WCS n".
5. **Core and UI speak indexes.** `WCS_SLOTS` leaves `camcraft-app` and
   `camcraft-ui`, apart from the two pre-v54 file migrations that need the old
   words to read old files.

## Out of scope

title: Build cycle: every worktree compiles the whole dependency tree cold - share a compile cache, cut debug info, use a faster linker

labels.description: Agent surface and tooling keep up with what shipped

body:
Raised by the maintainer (2026-11-11): "why are we cold building complete bundles .. the tests are localized to crates".

## What happens today (measured on the dev machine)
- Every issue worker, reviewer and gate works in its own worktree with its own `target/`. A fresh one compiles the WHOLE dependency tree before the first test runs: about 15-25 minutes per review and 25-75 minutes per gate, almost all of it third-party crates (flecs' C through bindgen/cc, wgpu/egui, the B-rep kernel, the script engine ...), not our code.
- `Cargo.toml` sets `[profile.dev.package."*"] opt-level = 2`: every dependency is optimised in dev builds. That makes tests run faster but makes each cold build much slower.
- Nothing sets `debug`, so dev builds carry full debug info for all crates: one `target/` reaches 50-120 GB (the disk filled twice today) and every link is slow.
- Integration tests are one binary per file: `crates/app/tests` has 266 files, motion 65, sim 50. The batch gate's app step takes about 24 of its 38 minutes, much of it linking and starting 266 binaries.
- `.cargo/config.toml` holds only the `xtask` alias: no linker choice, no cache wrapper. `sccache` is not installed; `rust-lld` is.

## Wanted (this issue: the three cheap ones, measured)
1. **A shared compile cache across worktrees** (`sccache` as `RUSTC_WRAPPER`, and as the C compiler wrapper for the cc-built C code if that works on MSVC). Registry crates live at the same path for every worktree, so their compilations are cache hits; a fresh worktree should then compile only our own crates. It must be OPTIONAL: a machine without sccache builds exactly as today (enable it from `cargo xtask` / the gate wrappers when `sccache` is on PATH, or document the env var - never hard-code a wrapper in `.cargo/config.toml` that breaks a machine without it). Say how to install it and how big its cache is allowed to grow.
2. **Less debug info**: `debug = false` (or `"line-tables-only"`) for dependencies, and line tables only for our crates in dev/test - enough for backtraces and panics with file:line. Report target size and link time before/after.
3. **A faster linker** for the Windows MSVC target (`rust-lld` / `lld-link`), and the equivalent on Linux/macOS where it helps, again without breaking a machine that lacks it.
4. Re-examine `opt-level = 2` for all dependencies: keep it only for the crates whose speed the tests need (measure: batch gate time with opt-level 2 everywhere vs 1 vs a short list).

Measure and report, on the same machine, cold (empty target, warm cache where a cache applies) and warm: `cargo test -p camcraft-app --no-run`, `cargo test -p camcraft-app --test <one binary>`, `cargo xtask gate quick` on a one-file app change, and the `target/` size. No test may change behaviour; the gates stay green.

## Not in this issue (file separately if the numbers say so)
- Folding the 266 one-file app test binaries into a few binaries (one per area, files as modules). This is the biggest structural win for the gate, but it changes the gate maps in `xtask` and every "run this binary" instruction.

## Process
`.cargo/config.toml`, `xtask/` and the gate wrappers are process files: bump `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION`, and say in the PR what a fork must do.

Done means: a fresh worktree reaches its first app test at least 3x faster than today with the cache warm, `target/` is at most half today's size, the settings are optional per machine and documented, and the measured numbers are in the PR.

body:
There's no thread-mill tool kind.

**Where:** `ToolKind` (`crates/tools/src/tools.rs:23`) has `Tap` and the lathe `Thread` insert, but no single-form or multi-form thread mill.

**Effect:** thread milling is a common job on small CNC mills (interpolated threads in any material, large or odd sizes, no tap breakage). A vendor tool library can't carry thread mills at all. In one real catalog build, over 300 thread mills had to be left out.

**Fix sketch:**
- New kinds: single-form (one tooth, any pitch within range) and multi-form (several teeth, a fixed pitch). Each carries cutter diameter, form angle, pitch or pitch range, teeth count, neck and shank.
- A thread-milling operation: helical interpolation, internal and external, climb or conventional, single or multi pass, radial passes.
- Simulation and gouge laws for the form.

Effort: max (a new kind, a helical op and the sim).

**Done means:** a thread mill can be stored and used by a thread-milling op that verifies clean and posts helical G2/G3 with Z; pinned with goldens.

  rotation: the frame comes from the plane dropdown, the point only
  moves the origin.

Selecting an entry expands its controls below the dropdown. Existing
functions are reused verbatim as the expanded content; the completing
work is the cylinder-angle backend and the per-setup origin placement.

## Everywhere the same

setup's orientation: the Setups overview (every setup stacked) and each
setup's own Settings page. Same dropdowns, same options, same look.

  existing tests stay green untouched).

  the chosen world axis with the typed angle about it; refusals by
  name (same face twice, coincident centroids, non-finite).
- The orientation point places the named setup's WCS origin (corner /

  undo restores. Inactive setups place their own WCS, not the active

title: Process changes - fork maintainers please subscribe

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: P?
labels.description: Paused: never picked until the maintainer sets a real priority

body:
**Subscribe to this issue** (the "Subscribe" button on the right) if you work from a fork of CamCraft, especially with an AI agent.

Forks sync product code only at release tags (AGENTS.md "A fork syncs from upstream at each cut tag"). But the *process* - `AGENTS.md`, the agent definitions in `.claude/agents/`, the skills in `.claude/skills/` and `scripts/gate.*` - changes between releases, and a fork's agents should follow the current rules (review labels, priority labels, release steps, and so on).

**How it works:**
- `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` holds one number. Every PR that changes a process file bumps it.
- Every such PR also adds a comment **here**: the new version, what changed, and what to pull. Subscribers get one notification per change.
- A fork's agent compares its `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` with upstream's at the start of each session and, if upstream is newer, pulls just the process files (AGENTS.md "Process files sync on every session"). Product code still waits for the next release tag.

**To pull by hand:**
```
git fetch upstream
git checkout upstream/main -- AGENTS.md .claude/agents .claude/skills .claude/PROCESS_VERSION scripts/gate.ps1 scripts/gate.sh
git commit -m "chore(process): sync process files to upstream PROCESS_VERSION <n>"
```

This issue stays open and pinned. It's labelled `P?` so no agent ever picks it up as work.

title: Launch terminal is silent while the app works - add real debug logging (tracing) to stdout

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: area:build
labels.description: Build, CI, release, tests

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:medium
labels.description: One module or crate, a known pattern (issue-worker-medium)

labels.name: P5
labels.description: Agent surface and tooling keep up with what shipped

body:
## What happens
When CamCraft is started from a terminal, the terminal tells you almost nothing
about what the app is doing. There is no logging framework in the workspace at
all: no `log` or `tracing` dependency in any Cargo.toml, no subscriber
init in the binaries - just ~185 ad-hoc `println!`/`eprintln!` calls scattered
across crates (cli.rs, gpu_init.rs, shell.rs, the post bin). If a subsystem
decides, refuses, retries, or fails to write a file, no line reaches the
console and the failure is only discovered later by forensics on the output.

## Why now (session of 2026-11-07)
Two incidents this week were diagnosed only by reading source afterwards,
because the console was silent during them:
- **A file did not get saved when post processing** - the post appeared to
  succeed; nothing in the terminal said which path it wrote (or that it wrote
  nothing at all).
- **A limit was hit while generating operations** - the generator aborted on a
  budget/limit; the terminal showed no trace of which cap fired or what the
  result was downgraded to.

Prime Directive says "log diagnostics, never silence" - today we cannot.

## Expected
The launching terminal streams debug-level logs of app activity, filterable:
- project save / post write: source path, destination, bytes, or the reason
  nothing was written;
- operation generation: start, end, duration, which limits/budgets stopped a
  generator and what fallback took over;
- verify/sim refusals: the rule that fired and the numbers behind it;
- commands executing (name + affected entities) at debug level.

## Suggested shape
`tracing` + `tracing_subscriber` fmt layer writing to stderr at startup of the
UI binary, default level `info`, overridable by `RUST_LOG` (or a camcraft
config/env of our own). Instrument the command dispatch seam, generators, and
post entry points - the crates are already split (M4.1), so each takes its own
span targets (`camcraft_app::post`, `camcraft_motion::adaptive`, ...). Keep
hot generation loops behind level gates - logging must not slow generation.

## Done means
- Launching the app and running a post writes terminal lines naming the file
  path and result; a failed/skipped write says why.
- Hitting a generation budget (e.g. an Adaptive limit) prints which limit and
  what happened next.
- Levels are controlled by env var, default output stays quiet at `info`, and
  the batch gate shows no measurable generation slowdown.

Found while debugging the post-save incident (user request, 2026-11-07).
